construction_notes: Default liquid wealth is the third-party-reported value of current accounts, savings accounts and securities accounts; available for the full population.

Reported liquid wealth starts from default liquid wealth and adds self-reported corrections; available only for individuals above the statutory retirement age, and it does not capture corrections made close to year-end, so it does not correspond completely to the variable the administration uses to evaluate the asset test.
Total wealth is default liquid wealth plus pension wealth and housing wealth and net of liabilities, which the authors say approximates total net wealth for this population.
Bank liquid wealth is the value of bank deposits and listed securities held at the bank; the cash adjustment adds in cash withdrawals made in the course of the month.

The statutory liquid wealth concept for the asset test covers balances on checking, savings and security accounts as well as cash, excludes consumer durables, real estate and pension accounts, and does not net out debt.

Observations from multiple years are pooled; before pooling, amounts are inflated to 2020 values with the average wage index the tax administration uses to adjust nominal parameters, including the wealth threshold of the old-age check, so that after indexation the relevant asset test threshold for all observations is the 2020 value (USD 1 = DKK 6.53).
Density figures group individuals into DKK 5,000 bins of liquid wealth; densities refer to the full distribution and not just the displayed portion.

Policy parameters: the old-age check is DKK 18,000 a year, paid in late January, means-tested against personal income with a DKK 42,000 disregard and a 34 percent phaseout rate for singles, and lost entirely when liquid wealth exceeds DKK 90,000. Social security parameters are reported for 2020.

The threshold of the asset test has been constant in real terms over the full period except for a 15 percent increase in 2010; the value of the check more than doubled in real indexed terms over the period of analysis (Supplemental Appendix Figure A.1).
